lessonTitle: Musculoskeletal Examination: Look, Feel, Move, the Knee and GALS

blocks.text: A 19-year-old footballer comes off the pitch holding his knee. He felt it 'give way' as he turned, heard a pop, and the joint swelled within two hours. Before any scan, a careful examination of how the knee looks, feels and moves can tell you which structure is most likely to be damaged.

blocks.markdown: Musculoskeletal (MSK) examination follows a consistent framework so that nothing is missed: **look, feel, move**, with **special tests** added for particular joints and a final assessment of **function**. You also **compare with the opposite side** and ask the patient about pain throughout, watching their face. This unit applies the framework to a joint, develops a knee examination including special tests, and introduces **GALS** (gait, arms, legs, spine), a quick screening examination of the whole locomotor system.

blocks.title: Look, feel, move
blocks.text: Look, feel, move is a three-step framework for examining any joint: inspect the joint and surrounding tissues (look), palpate for warmth, tenderness, swelling and crepitus (feel), then test active and passive range of movement (move), followed by special tests and a functional assessment.

blocks.markdown:
### Preparing and applying the framework

**Preparation**: wash your hands, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain and gain consent, expose the joint (and the joint above and below), ask about pain, and position the patient comfortably. Ask the patient to tell you immediately if anything hurts. Use a chaperone when appropriate.

**Look**: swelling, redness, deformity, scars, bruising, asymmetry, muscle wasting, and the posture or gait of the patient. Compare both sides.

**Feel**: with the back of the hand for temperature, then fingertips for tenderness along the joint line, bony landmarks and soft tissue; detect effusion and crepitus. Watch the patient's face.

**Move**: **active** movement (by the patient) first, then **passive** movement (by you) noting range, pain, crepitus and end-feel. Active movement tells you about function and pain, passive movement tells you about the joint itself. Always examine the joint above and below, for example the hip when a knee complaint exists, because hip disease can refer pain to the knee.

rows: Inspect standing and lying, both sides
Swelling, erythema, deformity (varus or valgus), wasting of quadriceps, scars
Warmth (inflammation or infection), joint-line tenderness (meniscus), effusion, crepitus
Active then passive flexion and extension
Range of movement, pain, crepitus, locking, fixed flexion deformity
Gait abnormality, antalgic gait, giving way
blocks.caption: Applying look, feel, move to the knee.

blocks.title: Examining a swollen knee
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old woman has had a swollen, painful right knee for three days after gardening. She has no fever. Describe how you apply look, feel and move to this knee.

steps.text: Look: with her standing and lying, expose both legs from groin to feet. Compare knees for swelling, redness, deformity (bow-leg or knock-knee), scars and wasting of the quadriceps. Observe her walk to see if she limps.

Feel: back of the hand to compare warmth over each knee. Palpate along the joint line and around the patella for tenderness. Test for effusion: a large effusion by the patellar tap (push the patella down and feel it tap against the femur), a small effusion by the bulge (sweep) test, in which fluid is milked from the medial side and a bulge appears on the medial side after pressing the lateral side.

Move: ask her to bend and straighten the knee (active), then bend it passively, with a hand on the patella to feel crepitus. Note the range from full extension (zero degrees) to flexion, any fixed flexion deformity, pain and the end-feel.
Then perform special tests and examine the hip, since hip pathology can refer to the knee. Finish by thanking the patient and washing your hands.

blocks.answer: A systematic comparison of both knees: inspect, palpate for warmth, effusion and joint-line tenderness, and assess active and passive range of movement before special tests, always including the hip.

blocks.markdown:
### Special tests of the knee

Special tests target specific structures. The most important are:

- **Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)**: the **anterior drawer test** (knee flexed to 90 degrees, foot stabilised, tibia pulled forward on the femur) and the **Lachman test** (knee flexed about 20 to 30 degrees, tibia pulled forward). Excess forward translation with a soft end-point suggests ACL injury. The Lachman test is generally more sensitive than the anterior drawer.
- **Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)**: the **posterior drawer test** (tibia pushed backwards at 90 degrees of flexion) and observing for a **posterior sag** of the tibia.
- **Collateral ligaments**: the **valgus stress test** (outward force on the lower leg with the knee slightly flexed, testing the medial collateral ligament) and the **varus stress test** (inward force, testing the lateral collateral ligament).
- **Menisci**: joint-line tenderness, locking, and the **McMurray test**: the flexed knee is rotated and then extended while feeling for a click or pain over the joint line, suggesting a meniscal tear.
- **Patella**: patellar tap and bulge tests for effusion, and the apprehension test for patellar instability.

items: Always test the normal knee first so you can compare laxity and avoid a surprise.
Relax the patient's hamstrings by supporting the leg, because muscle guarding can mask laxity.
A haemarthrosis (blood in the joint) soon after injury suggests ligament injury, a fracture or a meniscal tear in the vascular part.
Do not forget to examine the hip and ankle, and look at the whole limb.

blocks.title: Interpreting knee findings
blocks.prompt: The footballer in the hook has a large tense effusion within hours of injury, a positive Lachman test with a soft end-point, a negative posterior drawer and normal valgus and varus stress tests. Which structure is most likely damaged?

steps.text: Pattern recognition: a rapid effusion after twisting injury suggests bleeding into the joint (haemarthrosis), which occurs with injuries to well-vascularised structures such as the ACL.

Review the tests: a positive Lachman (excess anterior translation of the tibia with soft end-point) points to the ACL. A negative posterior drawer makes PCL injury unlikely, and normal valgus and varus stress tests make collateral ligament injury unlikely.
Consider associated injuries: ACL injuries are often accompanied by meniscal injury, so test joint-line tenderness and McMurray as well.
Conclude: this is most consistent with an ACL tear; the examination guides, but does not replace, imaging, and the patient should be referred appropriately.

blocks.markdown:
### GALS screening

GALS is a rapid screen (about five minutes) to detect musculoskeletal abnormalities and decide whether a detailed examination is needed. It has screening questions followed by inspection of **Gait, Arms, Legs and Spine**.

**Screening questions** (ask all three):
1. Do you have any pain or stiffness in your muscles, joints or back?
2. Can you dress yourself completely without difficulty?
3. Can you walk up and down stairs without difficulty?

**Gait**: watch the patient walk, turn and walk back, noting symmetry, stride, arm swing and any limp.

**Spine**: from behind, look for scoliosis, muscle bulk and alignment (shoulder, pelvic and skin-crease asymmetry); from the side, look at the cervical and lumbar curvature; ask the patient to bend sideways (neck and trunk), touch their toes (lumbar flexion should show smooth reversal of the lumbar lordosis) and look at the ceiling and over each shoulder.

**Arms**: with hands behind the head, hands stretched out in front, palms up and down, making a fist, squeezing the fingers (tender joints), and touching the tips of each finger with the thumb.

**Legs**: observe from the front for muscle bulk and alignment, check knee flexion and extension (feel for crepitus), internal rotation of the hips with the hips and knees flexed, and look at the feet and squeeze across the metatarsal heads.

blocks.title: Screening versus detailed examination
blocks.text: GALS is a screening tool: if a normal screen is combined with no symptoms, serious MSK disease is unlikely. Any abnormality leads to a regional examination of that part with look, feel, move and special tests.

blocks.title: Comfort and safety
blocks.text: Never force a painful joint through its range. Stop if the patient is distressed, avoid repeated testing of an acutely injured joint, and ask for senior help if you suspect a fracture or a septic joint (hot, swollen, very painful joint with fever) that needs urgent assessment.

points: Use look, feel, move on every joint, compare sides, and examine the joint above and below.
Active movement shows function and pain; passive movement tests the joint, noting range, crepitus and end-feel.

Knee special tests: Lachman or anterior drawer for ACL, posterior drawer for PCL, valgus and varus stress for collateral ligaments, McMurray for meniscus, and patellar tap or bulge tests for effusion.
GALS is a quick screen of gait, arms, legs and spine, beginning with three screening questions.
An abnormal GALS prompts a detailed regional examination.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the standard framework for examining a joint?

options.text: Look, feel, move, then special tests and function

questions.correctOptionText: Look, feel, move, then special tests and function

distractorRationale.a: Correct: standard order, followed by special tests and function.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: moving before inspecting or palpating may cause pain.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: special tests come after the basic framework.

questions.explanation: Inspection first avoids missing visible signs and does not cause pain, then palpation, then movement. Special tests and function build on these findings.

questions.stem: Which of the three GALS screening questions asks about function?

options.text: Can you dress yourself completely without difficulty?
Have you had any falls in the last year?
Are you allergic to any medicines?

questions.correctOptionText: Can you dress yourself completely without difficulty?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: one of the three standard GALS questions.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: falls history is useful but not one of the three.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: allergy history is not part of GALS.

questions.explanation: GALS begins with three questions about pain or stiffness, dressing, and stairs. Dressing and stairs test everyday function.

questions.stem: In an examination of the knee, the examiner flexes the knee to about 20 to 30 degrees and pulls the tibia forward on the femur, feeling excessive movement with a soft end-point. Which structure is suggested?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the Lachman test.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: PCL is tested by posterior drawer and posterior sag.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: menisci are tested by joint-line tenderness and McMurray.

questions.explanation: The Lachman test applies forward translation of the tibia with the knee slightly flexed and is positive when there is excessive movement with a soft end-point, indicating ACL injury.

questions.stem: A patient has pain on the medial side of the knee after a twisting injury. The knee is flexed, the lower leg is rotated and then extended, and the examiner feels a click with pain over the medial joint line. Which test is this and what does it suggest?

options.text: McMurray test, suggesting a meniscal tear
Valgus stress test, suggesting an ACL tear
Patellar tap, suggesting a small effusion
Posterior drawer, suggesting a PCL tear

questions.correctOptionText: McMurray test, suggesting a meniscal tear

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rotation with extension and a click or pain over the joint line.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: valgus stress tests the medial collateral ligament.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: patellar tap detects a large effusion, not a click.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: posterior drawer is a forward-and-backward translation test.

questions.explanation: McMurray test rotates the flexed knee and extends it, with a palpable click or pain at the joint line indicating a meniscal tear. Collateral and cruciate tests use different manoeuvres.

questions.stem: While performing the GALS spine assessment, the patient is asked to bend forward and touch their toes while you watch the lumbar spine. What is the normal finding?

options.text: The normal lumbar lordosis flattens and reverses smoothly into a gentle convex curve
The lumbar spine remains rigidly lordotic
The patient has a sideways bend only

questions.correctOptionText: The normal lumbar lordosis flattens and reverses smoothly into a gentle convex curve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: normal lumbar flexion reverses the lordosis.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: persistence of lordosis suggests restricted lumbar flexion.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the question concerns forward flexion.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the thoracic spine flexes forwards, not extends.

questions.explanation: A normal lumbar spine flexes so that the inward curve of lordosis flattens or reverses. Failure to do so suggests restricted lumbar movement, for example from pain or spondyloarthropathy.

questions.stem: On passive examination of a knee, you find a fixed flexion deformity so that the knee cannot extend beyond 10 degrees of flexion, and the maximum flexion is 120 degrees. What is the total arc of movement in degrees from the most extended to the most flexed position?
questions.explanation: The arc of movement is the maximum flexion minus the extension limit: 120 degrees minus 10 degrees equals 110 degrees. The fixed flexion deformity of 10 degrees reduces the arc compared with a normal knee, which moves from about 0 to around 135 to 140 degrees.

questions.stem: When examining a painful knee, you should also examine the hip, because hip disease can cause referred knee pain.
questions.explanation: The framework includes the joint above and below, because pain from the hip can be felt at the knee, particularly in children and older adults. Missing hip disease would lead to misdiagnosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a swollen knee after a fall. The posterior drawer test shows excessive backward movement of the tibia and the tibia appears to 'sag' backwards when the knee is flexed to 90 degrees. Which structure is most likely injured?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: posterior translation or sag indicates PCL injury.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: ACL injury causes excessive anterior translation.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: LCL is tested with varus stress.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the patellar tendon is tested by extension against resistance.

questions.explanation: The PCL prevents the tibia from moving backwards on the femur. A positive posterior drawer or posterior sag therefore indicates PCL injury.

questions.stem: Describe how you would perform a GALS screening examination, including the three screening questions and what you would check for in the gait and spine.
markingGuide: Three screening questions: pain or stiffness, dressing, stairs
Gait: observe walking, turning, symmetry, stride, arm swing and limp
Spine from behind: scoliosis, symmetry, muscle bulk
Spine from the side: normal curvature
Lateral flexion, forward flexion with reversal of lumbar lordosis, neck movements
Abnormal findings lead to detailed regional examination
questions.explanation: GALS combines three questions with a quick structured look at gait, arms, legs and spine. If there are no symptoms and the screen is normal, significant MSK disease is unlikely.

questions.stem: Describe the special tests you would perform to assess the ligaments and menisci of the knee after a twisting injury, and say which structure each test examines.
markingGuide: Lachman and anterior drawer for ACL
Posterior drawer and posterior sag for PCL
Valgus stress for medial collateral ligament
Varus stress for lateral collateral ligament
McMurray test and joint-line tenderness for menisci
Compares with the normal knee and explains the technique and end-point
questions.explanation: Each test stresses one structure: anterior and posterior translation for the cruciates, varus and valgus forces for the collaterals, and rotation with flexion and extension for the menisci. Comparing with the normal side is essential.
